summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive website that turns NASA Earth science visualizations into sound. It analyses colours and patterns in images showing wind, aerosols, and ocean temperatures, then converts the data into different sounds as users scan across the image.

Our project addresses the challenge of making Earth science data more accessible, especially for people who are blind or have low vision. Instead of relying only on visual information, users can listen to changes in the data through sound. The website also includes text-to-speech descriptions, instrument selection, volume controls, and interactive scanning to improve the experience.

Earth Jukebox offers a different way to explore our planet. It helps make scientific information more inclusive and gives more people the opportunity to experience and understand Earth's changing systems through sound.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Earth Jukebox is an interactive website that converts NASA Earth science visualizations into sound. It currently supports three types of data: wind patterns, atmospheric aerosols, and ocean temperatures.

The website analyses the colours and pixel patterns in each visualization using HTML Canvas and JavaScript. It then maps the analysed data to sound properties such as pitch, volume, and instrument. As users move across or scan different parts of an image, the sound changes to represent variations in the data. This allows users to explore Earth's systems through both sight and sound.

What benefits does it have?

Earth Jukebox provides an alternative way to understand scientific visualizations. It is especially useful for people who are blind or have low vision, as it reduces the need to rely entirely on visual information. Features such as text-to-speech, instrument selection, volume controls, and interactive scanning make the experience more accessible and customizable.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make Earth science more inclusive and easier to explore. We want more people, regardless of their visual abilities, to experience and understand the patterns and changes happening across our planet.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed the project as a web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used the HTML Canvas API to analyse image data, the Web Audio API to generate and control sounds, and a soundfont library for instrument-based audio. We also implemented text-to-speech using browser speech capabilities. NASA Earth visualization images were used as the scientific data sources. No special hardware is required; the project runs in a web browser with speakers or headphones.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting Earth data only through charts, colours, and images, Earth Jukebox transforms it into an interactive sound experience. Different scientific patterns are represented through different audio characteristics, allowing users to listen to the data and explore it in a new way. Combining scientific visualization, sound, and accessibility makes the project a creative approach to understanding our planet.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered accessibility, ease of use, meaningful sound representation, and the ability to support different types of Earth data. We also focused on making the experience interactive and customizable while keeping it simple enough to use in a normal web browser. Our aim was to create something that is not just a demonstration of sound generation, but a useful alternative way to experience Earth science.
